rawInput.complaint:
A 52-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of microscopic hematuria and a rise in creatinine from a baseline of 59 to 94 µmol/L. Over three months, she had developed a bilateral petechial rash on her lower extremities, intermittent right knee swelling and pain, and a two-year history of subjective fevers and night sweats. A short course of oral prednisone produced transient improvement in her rash and systemic symptoms, but these recurred on tapering. She was restarted on prednisone 30 mg daily one week before nephrology consultation for concern of vasculitis or connective tissue disease.

Her medical history included a left femoral crossover graft (2005), gastroesophageal reflux, dyslipidemia, depression, and at least six months of microscopic hematuria with normal cystoscopy. Medications were rabeprazole, ASA, simvastatin, citalopram, and bupropion. On exam, she had palpable petechiae on her lower extremities and warm moderate effusions in the right knee and ankle; vital signs were normal.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 102 g/L, WBC 11.1×10^9/L, creatinine 94 µmol/L, ESR 115 mm/hr, CRP 94 mg/L, and rheumatoid factor 176 IU/mL. Urinalysis had trace protein, 58 RBCs/HPF with acanthocytes, and 7 WBCs/HPF. ANCA, C3, and C4 were normal. A skin biopsy demonstrated leukocytoclastic vasculitis with dermal capillary IgM and C3 deposition. Knee arthrocentesis was noninfectious and noncrystalline.

Serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and syphilis were negative; blood cultures were negative. SPEP showed no monoclonal protein; cryoglobulins and anti-CCP were negative. Kappa and lambda light chains were modestly elevated. ANA was weakly positive with RNP 1.1 AI, dsDNA was negative, and lupus anticoagulant was normal. Twenty-four–hour urine protein was 0.32 g. Renal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys.

Because her creatinine and symptoms initially improved on prednisone, biopsy was deferred. Upon prednisone withdrawal, her creatinine rose to 111 µmol/L and symptoms recurred, prompting a renal biopsy. Light microscopy revealed diffuse global mesangial hypercellularity. Immunofluorescence showed trace mesangial IgG and kappa, 1+ IgM, lambda, and C1q, and 2+ C3. Electron microscopy demonstrated mesangial electron-dense deposits. These findings were thought to be consistent with mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis, although her clinical and serologic profile was atypical.

She was treated with prednisone and azathioprine, then mycophenolate mofetil, hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab in various combinations, each time showing creatinine improvement on steroids and relapse on tapering. Given her atypical clinical features and inability to wean prednisone, the lupus diagnosis was reconsidered. Repeat transthoracic echocardiogram, CT of the abdomen and pelvis, and blood cultures showed no infectious focus. She was referred for further infectious evaluation.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief problem is a glomerular renal process with systemic inflammatory features: microscopic hematuria with acanthocytes and rising creatinine, plus palpable petechial rash, intermittent oligoarthritis/effusions, and prolonged constitutional symptoms (subjective fevers and night sweats for two years). The patient’s own major concern appears to be a presumed vasculitic/connective tissue disease because symptoms improved with prednisone but repeatedly recurred when steroids were tapered.

Salient positive findings supporting an immune-complex systemic process include: palpable lower-extremity petechiae with skin biopsy showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis and dermal capillary IgM/C3 deposition; urinary RBCs with acanthocytes indicating glomerular bleeding; mild proteinuria (0.32 g/day); elevated inflammatory markers (ESR 115, CRP 94); anemia; elevated rheumatoid factor (176 IU/mL); and renal biopsy showing mesangial proliferative GN with mesangial electron-dense deposits and C3/C1q/IgM-predominant staining. She also had warm noninfectious, noncrystalline knee and ankle effusions, fitting immune-complex disease. A very important historical clue is the prior left femoral crossover graft in 2005, which creates a potential chronic endovascular infectious nidus.

Pertinent negatives help exclude several primary rheumatologic causes. ANCA was normal, arguing against ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis. Complements C3/C4 were normal, which is atypical for active lupus nephritis or mixed cryoglobulinemia. Hepatitis B/C and HIV were negative, making secondary cryoglobulinemic vasculitis less likely. Cryoglobulins were negative. ANA was only weakly positive, dsDNA negative, lupus anticoagulant normal, and anti-CCP negative; this is not a convincing lupus or rheumatoid arthritis serologic profile. SPEP showed no monoclonal protein, arguing against paraprotein-associated immune-complex disease. Arthrocentesis excluded septic and crystal arthritis. Repeated blood cultures and transthoracic echo were negative, but these do not fully exclude chronic culture-negative endovascular infection, especially if intermittent or involving prosthetic vascular material.

Differential diagnosis:
1. Lupus nephritis / SLE: The renal biopsy was interpreted as mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis because of mesangial hypercellularity with immune deposits including C1q. Skin leukocytoclastic vasculitis and arthritis can occur in SLE. However, the overall fit is poor: she is 52 with only weak ANA positivity, negative dsDNA, normal complements, no other classic lupus manifestations provided, and persistent constitutional symptoms over two years. Repeated relapse despite multiple immunosuppressive regimens and steroid dependence also argue that lupus is not the true underlying driver.
2. Cryoglobulinemic immune-complex vasculitis: This can cause palpable purpura, arthralgia/arthritis, glomerulonephritis, elevated RF, and immune-complex deposition. The high RF and leukocytoclastic vasculitis make this attractive. But cryoglobulins were negative, hepatitis C was negative, complements were normal rather than low, and the renal biopsy description is not classic membranoproliferative cryoglobulinemic GN.
3. IgA vasculitis: Palpable purpura, arthritis, and glomerular hematuria fit. But skin biopsy showed IgM/C3 rather than IgA deposition, and renal biopsy did not describe IgA-dominant mesangial deposits, making this less likely.
4. ANCA-associated vasculitis: Could explain rash, renal injury, and systemic symptoms, but ANCA was negative and biopsy showed immune-complex mesangial deposits rather than pauci-immune GN.
5. Subacute or chronic infective endovascular infection, particularly vascular graft infection with immune-complex glomerulonephritis and leukocytoclastic vasculitis: This best integrates the prolonged fevers/night sweats, elevated ESR/CRP, anemia, high RF, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, glomerular hematuria, immune-complex mesangial GN, and repeated steroid responsiveness with relapse when tapering. Chronic infection can produce false-positive/low-titer autoantibodies and mimic lupus. The prior femoral crossover graft is a major clue to a possible occult prosthetic vascular infection. Negative blood cultures and unrevealing transthoracic echo do not exclude this, especially for indolent organisms or localized graft infection.

Narrowing to the single most likely diagnosis: although the kidney biopsy was initially labeled mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis, the total clinical picture is atypical for lupus and much more suggestive of infection-associated immune-complex disease. The strongest unifying diagnosis is chronic vascular graft infection causing immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis and glomerulonephritis. This explains the constitutional symptoms over years, inflammatory markers, RF elevation, skin leukocytoclastic vasculitis, renal immune-complex deposits, and failure of durable remission with immunosuppression alone.
